title: Abraham Zacuto wrote astronomical tables in Hebrew, and the navigation tables for Vasco da Gama's voyage were computed with them

trailer.text: Abraham ben Samuel Zacuto was a Spanish-Jewish astronomer, mathematician and historian.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, he was certainly the author of the tables prepared for the voyage of Vasco da Gama.
In 1473, in Salamanca, Zacuto began writing a book of astronomical tables in Hebrew.
After the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492 he moved to Portugal, where he became court astronomer to King João II.
In 1496 the book was printed in Leiria in a Latin translation, under the title Almanach perpetuum.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, until 1537 all solar tables for navigation prepared in Portugal were computed from the book's figures.

paragraphs.text: Abraham Zacuto was born in Salamanca, Spain.
According to the Spanish Biographical Dictionary, his family had earlier lived in France.
In his book "Sefer Yuhasin", Zacuto noted that his grandfather came from France.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Zacuto was a Jew, and he studied medicine and astrology at the University of Salamanca.
The sources disagree on whether he also taught at the university.
According to an article by the University of Washington, in 1473, at the age of 21, Zacuto made sure there was no rabbinic prohibition against studying the movements of the sun and moon.
After that he began working on the Great Compilation (ha-Hibbur ha-Gadol).
According to the Spanish Biographical Dictionary, this was his first book of astronomy.
It includes rules and tables, and Zacuto wrote it in Hebrew for a Jewish audience.
According to the same dictionary, the tables begin in the year 1473, but Zacuto finished the work around 1478.
According to the University of Washington article, the book has 19 chapters and was completed in 1478.
According to the Spanish Biographical Dictionary, three years later Juan de Salaya translated the treatise into Castilian, with the help of Zacuto himself.
Juan de Salaya, who translated the treatise into Castilian, had previously, in 1464–1469, held the chair of astrology at Salamanca.

stations.title: Expulsion, and the royal court in Lisbon

paragraphs.text: According to the article, on March 13, 1492, Isabel I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon ordered that all Jews in Spain convert to Christianity or be expelled from their kingdoms.
According to the article, Zacuto refused to convert and left Salamanca.
He went to Portugal, where King João II welcomed him.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in Lisbon Zacuto was soon appointed court astronomer and chronicler to the king.
According to the University of Washington article, the next king, Manoel I, upheld his appointment.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, King John II was interested in developing the art of navigation, and quickly profited from Zacuto's presence.

stations.title: Tables and instruments for the open sea

paragraphs.text: According to the University of Washington article, the instruments that existed before Zacuto were unsuited to use on a rocking ship at sea.
According to the article, in Portugal Zacuto perfected the astrolabe, an instrument that measures the altitude of celestial bodies above the horizon.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the ships of Vasco da Gama's voyage were equipped with Zacuto's improved astrolabe.
According to the article, Zacuto charted the positions of celestial bodies in a form that was easy to read.
In this way navigators could calculate their distance from the equator and maintain their latitude on the open sea.

According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Zacuto continued to serve in his position under King Manuel, and in this position the king consulted him regarding the practicability of Vasco da Gama's projected expedition, which Zacuto approved and encouraged.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Zacuto was the author of the tables prepared for da Gama's voyage for the years 1497–1500.
The tables were computed from data in the Almanach perpetuum.
The University of Washington article opens by asking whether the reader has heard of the Sephardic astronomer who helped Columbus chart his course across the sea.
The article calls him "Columbus’ Jewish astronomer", who helped connect the two sides of the Atlantic Ocean.
According to the article, Columbus set sail in 1492, in the same month in which the Jews were expelled from Spain.
The book was printed by Abraham ben Samuel d'Ortas.
According to the Cervantes catalogue, d'Ortas worked as a printer in the years 1492–1496.
The book's title states that it was translated from Hebrew into Latin by Master Joseph Vizinho.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Vizinho also translated the work into Spanish and appended it to a book of his own.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, in one of the editions the introduction explaining how to use the tables was translated into Spanish.
According to the Spanish Biographical Dictionary, there was also a version with the rules in Castilian.
According to the University of Washington article, on December 5, 1496, King Manoel I signed a decree ordering the Jews to convert or leave.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, as a result of King Manoel's persecutions, Zacuto and his son Samuel were forced to flee to save their lives.
According to the article, Zacuto left Portugal in 1497, but a long time passed before he reached his next destination.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, on the way he was twice taken prisoner, and in the end he reached Tunis.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in 1504 in Tunis he wrote a history of the Jews from the Creation to 1500.
According to the University of Washington article, there he no longer composed major astronomical works, only a few small treatises.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, when the Spanish invaded Tunis he fled to Turkey.
According to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, until 1537 all solar tables for navigation prepared in Portugal were computed from the figures of the Almanach perpetuum.
According to the University of Washington article, his tables were reprinted and discussed in Latin, Spanish, Castilian, Arabic, Hebrew and even Ladino.
According to the article, in 1568 Daniel ben Perahia published a Ladino version of the book in Salonica, then part of the Ottoman Empire.
According to the article, his work influenced major figures in the history of Portugal, Italy and Spain.
The lunar crater Zagut is named after him.
The author of the article says that his scientific influence is not recognized enough today.
An original copy of the book is held in the Library of the University of Seville, and there is also a security microfilm of it.
In 2003 the Miguel de Cervantes Virtual Library in Alicante published a digital edition of it.
The New York Public Library holds an item of the book, and its title gives the base year 1473.
According to the University of Washington article, the privileges Zacuto received at the Spanish and Portuguese courts were temporary, and protected him only as long as he was considered useful.

According to the article, he did not know that his work would serve the Spanish monarchy and the settlement of the landmasses that came to be known as the Americas, and did not know that he himself would soon be exiled from his homeland.
According to the article, Columbus and his legacy have recently been re-examined, and sometimes even condemned.
The reason is his role in initiating the conquest of the Americas and in the displacement and extermination of indigenous peoples.

The chronicler Gaspar Correia wrote that Zacut brought the astrolabe to Portugal, but according to the Dictionary of Scientific Biography this part of his claim is surely incorrect, because the astrolabe had been known in Portugal since at least the 12th century.

disagreements.question: In what year was Zacuto born?

versions.says: The Dictionary of Scientific Biography: about 1450
The Biographical Dictionary of the Royal Academy of History: 1452

disagreements.question: Where and when did Zacuto die?

versions.says: The Jewish Encyclopedia: in Turkey, after 1510
The Dictionary of Scientific Biography: in Portugal, about 1522
The Spanish Biographical Dictionary: probably in Jerusalem, about 1515
The Jewish Encyclopedia: he was appointed professor at the University of Salamanca, and later at the University of Saragossa
The Dictionary of Scientific Biography: several historians have claimed that he held a chair in Salamanca, but no document confirming this has yet been found
The Spanish Biographical Dictionary: there is no proof that he studied or taught at the University of Salamanca

disagreements.question: What material was Zacuto's improved astrolabe made of?

versions.says: The Jewish Encyclopedia: iron, and it was the first to be made of iron instead of wood
The University of Washington article: he perfected the model of the astrolabe in copper

disagreements.question: How many versions of the book were printed in Leiria in 1496?

versions.says: The Dictionary of Scientific Biography: two editions
The Spanish Biographical Dictionary: three versions, two with the rules in Latin and one in Castilian

unknowns.text: The book Zacuto wrote in 1473 appears under different names: "Bi'ur Luḥot" according to the Jewish Encyclopedia, and the Great Compilation (ha-Hibbur ha-Gadol) according to other sources. The sources do not say explicitly whether it is the same book

An article by the Sephardic Studies Program at the University of Washington calls Zacuto "Columbus’ Jewish astronomer", himself a victim of persecution, and writes that he helped connect the two worlds on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, אחרי מסע רצוף תלאות שבו נתפס פעמיים בשבי הגיע זקות לתוניס, ומשם נמלט לטורקיה בעת הפלישה הספרדית.
claims.quote: After an eventful voyage in which he was twice taken prisoner, Zacuto reached Tunis, where he lived until the Spanish invasion, when he fled to Turkey

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, ב-1504, בעת שהותו בתוניס, כתב זקות היסטוריה כרונולוגית של היהודים מבריאת העולם עד 1500.
claims.quote: In 1504, during his sojourn at Tunis, he wrote a chronological history of the Jews from the Creation to 1500, making constant reference to Jewish literature

claims.text: לפי המאמר, בתוניסיה לא חיבר זקות עוד יצירות אסטרונומיות מרכזיות, אלא רק כמה חיבורים אסטרונומיים.
claims.quote: Once in Tunisia, Zacuto composed no further major astronomical works, only a few astronomical treatises.

claims.text: לפי המאמר, לוחות האסטרונומיה של זקות הודפסו מחדש ונדונו בלטינית, ספרדית, קסטיליאנית, ערבית, עברית ואפילו בלאדינו.
claims.quote: Zacuto’s astronomical tables, however, were re-printed and discussed in Latin, Spanish, Castilian, Arabic, Hebrew, and even in Ladino.

claims.text: לפי המאמר, ב-1568 בסלוניקי, אז חלק מהאימפריה העות'מאנית, פרסם דניאל בן פרחיה גרסה בלאדינו של Almanah Perpetuum.
claims.quote: In 1568, in the city of Salonica, located all the way on the eastern end of the Mediterranean and then part of the Ottoman Empire, Daniel ben Perahia published a Ladino version of Almanah Perpetuum.

claims.text: לפי המאמר, יצירתו של זקות השפיעה על דמויות מרכזיות בהיסטוריה הפורטוגזית, האיטלקית והספרדית.
claims.quote: His work proved to be influential on major figures within Portuguese, Italian, and Spanish history

claims.text: לדברי כותבת המאמר, השפעתו המדעית של זקות אינה מוכרת כיום מספיק, אך עבודתו אפשרה את מסעותיו המפורסמים של קולומבוס.
claims.quote: His scientific influence is not recognized much today, but nevertheless, this Sephardic astronomer’s work made the famous voyages of Columbus possible

claims.text: לפי קטלוג סרוונטס, העותק המקורי של הספר נמצא בספריית אוניברסיטת סביליה, ויש לו גם מיקרופילם ביטחון.
claims.quote: Ubicación de originales: Biblioteca de la Universidad de Sevilla. También disponible como microfilm de seguridad

claims.text: הספרייה הווירטואלית מיגל דה סרוונטס באליקנטה פרסמה ב-2003 מהדורה דיגיטלית של הספר.
claims.quote: Publicación: Alicante : Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes, 2003

claims.text: בספרייה הציבורית של ניו יורק (ספריות דיגיטליות) מופיע פריט Almanach perpetuum celestium motuum של האסטרונום זקות, ובכותרתו צוין שנת הבסיס (Radix) 1473.
claims.quote: Almanach [?]petuu[ue] celestiu[ue] motuu[ue] / astronomi zacuti. Cui[us] Radix est / 1 4 7 3 /

claims.text: לפי המאמר, ההטבות שקיבל זקות בחצרות ספרד ופורטוגל היו זמניות והגנו עליו רק כל עוד נראה מועיל.
claims.quote: Despite Zacuto having had privileges in the Spanish and Portuguese courts through his work, those privileges were temporary and only afforded him protection

claims.text: לפי המאמר, זקות לא ידע שתרומתו תשמש את המלוכה הספרדית, שהוא עצמו יגורש בקרוב מארצו, ושחיבוריו ישמשו ליישוב היבשות שנודעו כאמריקה.
claims.quote: he would soon be exiled from his homeland, and his treatises would be put to use to colonize the landmasses that came to be known as the Americas.

claims.text: לפי המאמר, קולומבוס ומורשתו עומדים לאחרונה בשיקול מחדש, אף בגינוי, בשל תפקידו בפתיחת כיבוש אמריקה ובעקירת ובהשמדת עמים ילידים.
claims.quote: for his role in initiating the conquest of the Americas and the displacement and extermination of indigenous peoples across the continents.

claims.text: לפי מילון הביוגרפיה המדעית, הטענה של גספר קוריאה שזקות הכניס את האסטרולב לפורטוגל היא בוודאי שגויה, כי האסטרולב היה מוכר בפורטוגל לפחות מהמאה ה-12.
claims.quote: Al thought the first aprt of his claim si surely incorret (the astroalbe had been known in Portugal since at least the twelgth century)

claims.text: לפי מילון הביוגרפיה המדעית, זקות נולד בסלמנקה שבספרד בסביבות 1450 ונפטר בפורטוגל בסביבות 1522.
claims.quote: (b. Salamanca, Spain ca. 1450; d. Portugal, ca, 1522)

claims.text: הכרוניקן גספר קוריאה כתב שזקות הביא את האסטרולב לפורטוגל, אבל לפי מילון הביוגרפיה המדעית החלק הזה בטענתו בוודאי שגוי, כי האסטרולב היה מוכר בפורטוגל לפחות מהמאה ה-12.
claims.quote: the astroalbe had been known in Portugal since at least the twelgth century

claims.text: לפי מילון הביוגרפיה המדעית, המלך ז'ואאו השני התעניין בפיתוח אמנות הניווט, והפיק במהירות תועלת מנוכחותו של זקות.
claims.quote: Zacuto went ot Portugal whree he wsa welcomed by John II (1492).
